source: Synaptic inputs to cortical neurons are highly structured in adult sensory systems, such that neighboring synapses along dendrites are activated by similar stimuli.

source: This organization of synaptic inputs, called synaptic clustering, is required for high-fidelity signal processing, and clustered synapses can already be observed before eye opening.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the functional importance of synaptic clustering.

claim: Clustered synapses can already be observed before eye opening.
source: This organization of synaptic inputs, called synaptic clustering, is required for high-fidelity signal processing, and clustered synapses can already be observed before eye opening.

claim: The frequency of transmission events increases several fold during the second postnatal week until eye opening.
source: We found that the number of functional synapses and the frequency of transmission events increase several fold during this developmental period.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

source: At the beginning of the second postnatal week, synapses assemble specifically in confined dendritic segments, whereas other segments are devoid of synapses.

evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: Developing neurons select their synaptic partners based on molecular cues such as adhesion molecules.
source: Developing neurons select their synaptic partners based on molecular cues such as adhesion molecules and subsequently refine their connections through activity-dependent synaptic plasticity, stabilization and elimination driven by spontaneous network activity, and later, after the onset sensory function, by experience (Cline, 2003; Martini et al., 2021; Sanes and Zipursky, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Developing neurons refine their connections through activity-dependent synaptic plasticity, stabilization and elimination driven by spontaneous network activity.
source: Developing neurons select their synaptic partners based on molecular cues such as adhesion molecules and subsequently refine their connections through activity-dependent synaptic plasticity, stabilization and elimination driven by spontaneous network activity, and later, after the onset sensory function, by experience (Cline, 2003; Martini et al., 2021; Sanes and Zipursky, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Excitatory synapses between neurons emerge during the end of the first postnatal week in mouse and rat sensory cortex.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that excitatory synapses between neurons emerge during the end of the first postnatal week in mouse and rat sensory cortex (Blue and Parnavelas, 1983; De Felipe et al., 1997; Miller and Peters, 1981; Wildenberg et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior electron microscopy studies.

claim: The addition of new synapses peaks at the end of the second postnatal week.
source: The addition of new synapses peaks at the end of the second postnatal week and synapse density in the primary visual and somatosensory cortices approaches adult levels once the eyes open at postnatal day (P) 14 (Blue and Parnavelas, 1983; De Felipe et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Synapse density in the primary visual and somatosensory cortices approaches adult levels once the eyes open at postnatal day (P) 14.
source: The addition of new synapses peaks at the end of the second postnatal week and synapse density in the primary visual and somatosensory cortices approaches adult levels once the eyes open at postnatal day (P) 14 (Blue and Parnavelas, 1983; De Felipe et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Synaptic inputs of cortical pyramidal cells are clustered, such that synapses with similar activity patterns or stimulus selectivity are located near each other along their dendrites.
source: Recent studies demonstrated that synaptic inputs of cortical pyramidal cells are clustered, such that synapses with similar activity patterns or stimulus selectivity are located near each other along their dendrites (Iacaruso et al., 2017; Ju et al., 2020; Kerlin et al., 2019; Otor et al., 2022; Scholl et al., 2021; Takahashi et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2016; Winnubst et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple recent studies.

claim: Pyramidal cell dendrites integrate local inputs supra-linearly.
source: Since pyramidal cell dendrites integrate local inputs supra-linearly (Branco and Häusser, 2011; Harnett et al., 2012; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Makara and Magee, 2013), this arrangement of clustered inputs is thought to allow for local synaptic integration in dendritic computational subunits (Larkum, 2022; Larkum and Nevian, 2008; Major et al., 2013; Tran-Van-Minh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The arrangement of clustered inputs allows for local synaptic integration in dendritic computational subunits.
source: Since pyramidal cell dendrites integrate local inputs supra-linearly (Branco and Häusser, 2011; Harnett et al., 2012; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Makara and Magee, 2013), this arrangement of clustered inputs is thought to allow for local synaptic integration in dendritic computational subunits (Larkum, 2022; Larkum and Nevian, 2008; Major et al., 2013; Tran-Van-Minh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents an inference from the cited work.

claim: Local dendritic integration dramatically increases the computational power of neurons.
source: Local dendritic integration dramatically increases the computational power of neurons (Poirazi and Mel, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Experimentally blocking supra-linear dendritic integration disturbs sensory stimulus sensitivity and selectivity in cortical neurons.
source: Furthermore, experimentally blocking supra-linear dendritic integration disturbs sensory stimulus sensitivity and selectivity in cortical neurons (Lavzin et al., 2012; Palmer et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Learning is associated with structural plasticity of clustered synapses.
source: Finally, learning is associated with structural plasticity of clustered synapses (Cichon and Gan, 2015; Fu et al., 2012; Hedrick et al., 2022; Makino and Malinow, 2011; McBride et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Synaptic clustering can be observed early on in the developing visual system of tadpoles and mice.
source: Synaptic clustering can be observed early on in the developing visual system of tadpoles and mice (Podgorski et al., 2021; Winnubst et al., 2015), suggesting that synaptic inputs develop with some degree of specificity, but the trajectory of functional synaptic input development has been unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The study imaged 12 dendritic areas from 11 mice at ages between postnatal days 8–13.
source: Calcium transients at individual synapses reflecting synaptic transmission (Jia et al., 2010; Takahashi et al., 2012; Winnubst et al., 2015) allowed us to map synaptic inputs across 12 dendritic areas from 11 mice at ages between postnatal days 8–13, the day before eye opening.
evidence: This describes the experimental sample size and age range.

claim: The dendrites hosted 354 functional synapses, which produced 3440 synaptic transmission events.
source: Together, these dendrites hosted 354 functional synapses, which produced 3440 synaptic transmission events.
evidence: This describes the total number of synapses and events observed in the study.

claim: In the mature cortex, most excitatory synapses of pyramidal neurons are located on spines.
source: In the mature cortex, most excitatory synapses of pyramidal neurons are located on spines (Berry and Nedivi, 2017; Kasai et al., 2021; Moyer and Zuo, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: During development, many cortical synapses are formed directly onto the shaft.
source: However, during development, many cortical synapses are formed directly onto the shaft (Miller and Peters, 1981; Wildenberg et al., 2023), where synaptic calcium transients are masked by calcium influx triggered by back-propagating action potentials.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The density of functional synapses increased significantly between P8 and P13.
source: In line with these previous EM studies, we report here that the density of functional synapses increased significantly between P8 and P13 (Figure 3A and B).

claim: The frequency of synaptic transmission at individual synapses increased during the second postnatal week.
source: The frequency of synaptic transmission at individual synapses increased as well (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The number of synaptic transmission events in a given dendrite was higher by P12/13 compared to the beginning of the second postnatal week (P8–10).
source: Hence, the number of synaptic transmission events in a given dendrite was higher by P12/13 (n = 6 dendrites) compared to the beginning of the second postnatal week (P8–10; n = 6 dendrites; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

source: While the percentage of spine synapses was slightly higher in older dendrites, there was no significant relationship between age and the percentage of spine synapses across the sampled dendrites (Figure 3E).

claim: Spine development is maximal after P14.
source: This is in line with previous observations that spine development is maximal after P14 (summarized in Lohmann and Kessels, 2014).

claim: Spine synapses were more active than shaft synapses in both young (P8–10) and older animals (P12–13).
source: In general, spine synapses were more active than shaft synapses in both young (P8–10; 0.55 ± 0.09 min–1 vs. 0.16 ± 0.03 min–1, mean ± SEM) and older animals (P12–13; 0.67 ± 0.07 min–1 vs. 0.23 ± 0.03 min–1; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A fraction of structural spines remained inactive during recordings in both younger (25 ± 20%) and older dendrites (9 ± 9%).
source: While we detected synaptic transmission at the majority of spines, a fraction of structural spines remained inactive during our recordings in both younger (25 ± 20%) and older dendrites (9 ± 9% for recording durations of 29 ± 8 and 26 ± 6 min, respectively; mean ± STD), possibly representing presynaptically silent synapses (Voronin and Cherubini, 2004).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data, with a citation suggesting a possible interpretation.

claim: Most synaptic inputs occurred in barrages (59% in young neurons, 61% in older neurons).
source: We found that most synaptic inputs occurred in barrages (59% in young neurons, 61% in older neurons).

claim: There was a trend toward an increase in synaptic charge transferred per barrage during development.

evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of synaptic transmission events per barrage during development.

evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The number of events observed per barrage correlated highly linearly with the charge transferred during each barrage.
source: As expected, the number of events observed per barrage correlated highly linearly with the charge transferred during each barrage (Figure 4E).

source: In addition, the amplitude of individual synaptic transmission events was higher during larger barrages (Figure 4F), suggesting that multiple synaptic vesicles were released simultaneously during larger barrages.

claim: Local co-activity drives plasticity to cluster neighboring synapses.
source: Since we had discovered previously that local co-activity drives plasticity to cluster neighboring synapses (Niculescu et al., 2018; Winnubst et al., 2015) and found here that the synapses within domains were more synchronized with their neighbors than the synapses located outside domains (Figure 6F), we examined whether co-activity of neighboring synapses within domains predicted changes in their activity levels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies by the authors.

claim: The Mann–Kendall score was more negative outside than inside domains, indicating that on average synapses outside domains tended to decrease in activity over time, whereas those inside domains showed a more positive activity trajectory.

claim: Each synapse's Mann–Kendall score of synaptic plasticity correlated positively with its local co-activity within 10 µm proximally and distally along the dendrite.
source: Next, we compared each synapse's Mann–Kendall score of synaptic plasticity with its local co-activity within 10 µm proximally and distally along the dendrite and revealed a significant positive correlation (Figure 7A and C), demonstrating that synapses that were synchronized with their neighbors became stabilized or more active compared to those that were out of sync with their neighbors.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figures 7A and C.

claim: Synapses that were synchronized with their neighbors became stabilized or more active compared to those that were out of sync with their neighbors.
source: Next, we compared each synapse's Mann–Kendall score of synaptic plasticity with its local co-activity within 10 µm proximally and distally along the dendrite and revealed a significant positive correlation (Figure 7A and C), demonstrating that synapses that were synchronized with their neighbors became stabilized or more active compared to those that were out of sync with their neighbors.

claim: Visual cortex neurons established functional synapses at a very high rate during the week leading up to eye opening.
source: Together, these findings showed that visual cortex neurons established functional synapses at a very high rate during the week leading up to eye opening and suggest that developing synapses became organized into functional, spatially distinct domains based on the synchronicity with their neighbors (Figure 7D).

claim: Developing synapses became organized into functional, spatially distinct domains based on the synchronicity with their neighbors.

claim: The distribution of synaptic transmission frequencies observed is most likely determined by release probability differences between individual presynaptic terminals along the dendrite.
source: In contrast, the largest population of input neurons (i.e., other layer 2/3 pyramidal cells) show very homogeneous firing activity during neonatal spontaneous network events where all neurons participate at a similar rate (Rochefort et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2012). Consequently, the distribution we observed here for individual synapses is most likely determined by release probability differences between individual presynaptic terminals along the dendrite.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings combined with cited prior work.

source: We used 11 C57BL/6J mouse pups between P8 and P13.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in layer 2/3 of the visual cortex were transfected with GCaMP6s and DsRed at E16.5 using in utero electroporation.
source: Pyramidal neurons in layer 2/3 of the visual cortex were transfected with GCaMP6s (2 mg/ml) and DsRed (0.5–2 mg/ml) at E16.5 using in utero electroporation (Winnubst et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: Low-level anesthesia does not change the basic properties of spontaneous network activity, such as participation rates and event amplitudes.
source: We previously reported that although this low level of anesthesia does reduce the frequency of spontaneous network events, relative to that seen in awake animals, it does not change the basic properties of spontaneous network activity, such as participation rates and event amplitudes (Siegel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Synaptic inputs are organized very similarly in vivo under light anesthesia and in slice cultures.
source: Furthermore, we found previously that synaptic inputs are organized very similarly in vivo under light anesthesia and in slice cultures (Winnubst et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The activity patterns investigated in this study are not or only slightly affected by low-level anesthesia.
source: Together, these observations indicate that the activity patterns investigated here are not or only slightly affected by low-level anesthesia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited prior work.

claim: The total dendritic length imaged per neuron was almost 10 times larger than in a previous study.
source: The total dendritic length imaged per neuron was almost 10 times larger than in our previous study (Winnubst et al., 2015), allowing us to map the large-scale distribution of synapses along developing dendrites.
evidence: This describes an improvement in the current study's methodology compared to prior work.

claim: Calcium transients at individual synapses reflect synaptic transmission.
source: Calcium transients at individual synapses reflecting synaptic transmission (Jia et al., 2010; Takahashi et al., 2012; Winnubst et al., 2015) allowed us to map synaptic inputs across 12 dendritic areas from 11 mice at ages between postnatal days 8–13, the day before eye opening.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies establishing this method.
